question: to the Commission Christophe Clergeau (S&D), Jutta Paulus (Verts/ALE), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Martin Hojsík (Renew) Subject:

According to a recent analysis by the non-governmental organisation ChemSec1, several major European chemical companies – including AkzoNobel, Arkema, BASF, Evonik, Henkel, Solvay, Syensqo, TotalEnergies, Umicore and Yara – fail to carry out a comprehensive double materiality assessment, as required under the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive2 (CSRD). The analysis indicates that some companies either omit the issue, conclude that hazardous chemicals are not material to their environmental impact or do not publish in accordance with legal requirements, raising concerns about the application of the CSRD reporting framework. 1.
Is the Commission aware of these shortcomings in the application of the CSRD, in particular regarding the reporting of hazardous substances?
How does the Commission assess Member States’ enforcement of the CSRD?
What will the Commission do to provide further guidance or clarification on reporting obligations concerning hazardous substances under the CSRD?

answer: (English version) to the Commission Christophe Clergeau (S&D), Jutta Paulus (Verts/ALE), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Martin Hojsík (Renew) (17 March 2026) Subject: Reporting obligations concerning hazardous substances under the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive According to a recent analysis by the non-governmental organisation ChemSec (1), several major European chemical companies — including AkzoNobel, Arkema, BASF, Evonik, Henkel, Solvay, Syensqo, TotalEnergies, Umicore and Yara — fail to carry out a comprehensive double materiality assessment, as required under the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (2) (CSRD). The analysis indicates that some companies either omit the issue, conclude that hazardous chemicals are not material to their environmental impact or do not publish in accordance with legal requirements, raising concerns about the application of the CSRD reporting framework. 1. Is the Commission aware of these shortcomings in the application of the CSRD, in particular regarding the reporting of hazardous substances? 2.
How does the Commission assess Member States’ enforcement of the CSRD?

3. What will the Commission do to provide further guidance or clarification on reporting obligations concerning hazardous substances under the CSRD? (28 May 2026) The rules introduced by the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (1) (CSRD) in the Accounting Directive (2) and in the Transparency Directive (3) must be transposed into national law and implemented by Member States. Possible concerns regarding the CSRD reporting by chemical companies should therefore be addressed to the national authorities or bodies in charge of ensuring compliance with national measures transposing the sustainability reporting rules. Under Article 6 of the CSRD as amended by Directive (EU) 2026/470 (4), the Commission is required to submit a report to the European Parliament and the Council by 30 April 2029 on the implementation of the CSRD, assessing related achievements, including the convergence of reporting practices among Member States. This report will enable assessing how Member States enforce sustainability reporting rules. The Commission will assess if additional guidance regarding the reporting of hazardous substances and any other issues regarding the simplified European Sustainability Reporting Standards is required, in light of demand from stakeholders and evidence-based practical experience of application of the standards.
